doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Adding new music to jazz with the Jazz Prophets
summary: Gardner describes the sextet's hard bop-rooted concept, varied textures, and its commitment to original compositions.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I saw a quote from your website that had to do with introducing new music to the jazz genre. Do you feel that’s part of your goal, your mission?

Oh without a doubt. Without a doubt you know. You can only play “All the Things You Are” but so many times you know, along with all the other great standards that have been put out there. And there are even a lot of tunes by — preexisting tunes that haven’t been played a lot, tunes like a tune by Miles Davis and Wayne Shorter, who wrote “ESP” on that Miles Davis record; or other Wayne Shorter stuff like “El Gaucho” by Herbie Hancock or Gigi Gryce or anybody you know. But nonetheless, we have something to say, within the Jazz Prophets as composers. And I use that sextet in order to provide a vehicle for that. And we have three CD’s out and actually one more is in the can, of new music. And so in order for the music to continually progress I believe that you have to keep adding to the genre in order to just keep it fresh. You know, the kind of the musical concept of my group is heavily steeped in the hard bop tradition you know. Because of our instrumentation we kind of, it’s very easy for us to kind of come out of the Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers kind of a format, although we don’t do any of that music because of the texture of the — because of the instrumentation, the texture kind of sounds the same with the trumpet, trombone and tenor saxophone, but we change that texture quite a bit, sometimes I have — on the tenor saxophone is Rob Dixon, we have him playing an alto or soprano saxophone, and even sometimes having my brother Vincent playing euphonium, you know, and me playing the trumpet or flugelhorn, changing the texture of it. And we’re writing in a different vein than was done during the hard bop era. So in keeping with this new era I guess that some historians have called neo-traditional or neo-classic jazz or whatever, you know, there’s a lot of new music out here you know. And it’s good music. We wouldn’t play it unless it was good you know.
